html:
A Roman law of 9 CE that rewarded upper-class citizens for marrying and having children and penalised those who did not. It was part of Augustus's effort to rebuild the old Roman families, which he thought were dying out.

It added to his earlier laws of 18 and 17 BCE on marriage and on adultery. Unmarried and childless people lost the right to receive all or part of inheritances left to them by people outside their family. Parents gained advantages: men with children moved faster up the ladder of offices, and a freeborn woman with three children, or a freed slave woman with four, no longer needed a male guardian to manage her property. This right was called the right of three children.

The law was named after the two consuls of 9 CE, Papius and Poppaeus, who, as the historian Cassius Dio noted, were both unmarried and childless. The equites protested against the rules, and they did little to raise the birth rate. Parts of them lasted for centuries, until Constantine dropped the penalties on the unmarried in 320.
sum: A Roman law of 9 CE that rewarded upper-class citizens for marrying and having children and penalised those who did not. It was part of Augustus's effort to rebuild the old Roman families, which he thought were dying out.
